item.title: How to Wake Foil Behind a Boat: A Beginner’s Guide
item.dc:creator: AFS
item.description: How to wake foil behind a boat: the gear to start with, boat speed, your first start in the water and safety. Foils made in France, 2-year warranty.
item.content:encoded: To wake foil, you ride a foil board behind a boat, holding a rope. The boat gives you the speed, so you need no wind. Once the board lifts, it flies above the water on the foil. This guide walks you through your first session: the gear, the boat, the start in the water and safety. To see the gear we recommend, go to our wake foil page. You need a boat and a driver, a tow rope, a wakefoil board and a complete foil: front wing, stabilizer, fuselage and mast. We recommend one setup: the Silk V2 front wing with the Pulse wakefoil board. You pick your Silk V2 size from your weight. Be clear on one…

item.title: Parawing Size Chart: Pick Your Size by Wind and Weight
item.dc:creator: AFS
item.description: Parawing size chart: wind sets your Stow size, your weight sets your front wing and board. Charts in kg and lb, plus our foil finder for your setup.
item.content:encoded: Pick your parawing size based on wind. Your weight sets the size of your front wing and your board. These are two separate choices, so make them one at a time. To see all the gear for this discipline, visit our parawing page. Our parawing, the Stow, comes in three sizes. We recommend changing sizes based on wind only. Your usual wind is between 15 and 30 knots? Go with the 3.5 m². You mostly ride in light wind, between 12 and 25 knots? Go with the 4.5 m². In strong wind, between 25 and 40 knots? Go with the 2.5 m². Torn between two sizes? An AFS expert helps you choose based on your weight…

You fly it with a short bar or handles, attached by lines of 1.3 to 1.8 m (4 to 6 ft). Parawinging is done on a foil. If you have never flown one, take lessons with an…

item.title: Foil Surfing Safety: Rules from the Lineup to the Fall
item.dc:creator: AFS
item.description: Foil surfing safety: pick your spot, fall away from the foil, wear a helmet and leash, respect right of way. AFS tips to check before every session.
item.content:encoded: In foil surfing, safety comes down to five things: pick an easy spot, learn to fall away from your foil, wear the right gear, use a leash and follow right-of-way rules in the lineup. item.title: What Is Wing Foiling (Winging)? Gear, Wind and First Steps
item.dc:creator: AFS
item.description: Wing foiling, or winging: you hold a wing and ride a foil board above the water. Gear, wind and first steps for a new wing foiler.
item.content:encoded: Wing foiling is a water sport where you hold an inflatable wing in your hands and ride a board fitted with a foil. The foil is a hydrofoil: a mast, a fuselage and two small carbon wings under the board. The wind pulls you through the wing. item.content:encoded: HR, HM, UHM or UHM Skinny: all four of our masts are carbon. To pick yours, you only need two numbers: your weight and the span of your biggest front wing. item.title: Foil: Should You Choose Carbon or Aluminum?
item.dc:creator: AFS
item.description: Foil: carbon or aluminum? Weight, stiffness, saltwater care and durability compared, and what we recommend for beginners. 2-year warranty, foils made in France.
item.content:encoded: Foil: should you choose carbon or aluminum? We recommend carbon. It’s lighter, it allows a thinner profile, and it doesn’t corrode. Aluminum usually costs less up front and handles knocks well. But it’s heavier and needs more care. That holds true for wing foiling, surf foiling and towed foiling alike. At AFS, every mast we make is carbon. You’ll find the full range on our All foils page. A foil is made of a mast, a fuselage, a front wing and a stabilizer. item.description: Wing foil pumping explained: how to take off in light winds when the breeze is weak. Learn the pumping wingfoil technique, with tips from AFS.
item.content:encoded: Getting started with wingfoiling in ideal weather conditions is great! But have you ever tried to take off in light winds? You know that frustration of being stuck on the surface of the water! Worse still, not even being able to stand up on your board! Or simply wanting to take off faster! The solution? Pumping! This technique will help you generate enough speed to finally take off. But also to maintain your momentum. Learn to master the pumping technique with these tips and tricks, and you’ll probably be able to treat yourself to even more great sessions! Progressing in wingfoil will become…

item.title: The best winter wingfoil spots and schools
item.dc:creator: AFS
item.description: Winter wing foil spots: wingfoiling can be enjoyed all year round. Find ideal places and schools to ride in winter, for beginners and experts. By AFS.
item.content:encoded: Wingfoiling is an exciting activity that can be enjoyed all year round, including in winter. Here are some ideal spots to enjoy this sport, for beginners and experts alike. Gruissan, located on the Mediterranean coast of France, is a prime location for wingfoiling thanks to its beautiful scenery and favorable wind conditions. Here is a selection of spots suitable for beginners and experts. For warm water, see our guides to Dakhla, Fuerteventura and Mauritius, or browse all our wing foil destinations.

item.title: How to do a wingfoil jibe?
item.dc:creator: AFS
item.description: Wing foil jibe: both methods step by step, the mistakes that make you fall and how to fix them, plus the gear that helps you learn.
item.content:encoded: A wing foil jibe (also spelled “gybe,” and you will see “wingfoil” written as one word) is a downwind turn that takes you onto the other tack without stopping or dropping off the foil. You turn away from the wind, flip the wing to the other side and change your feet. There are two ways to do it: switch your feet after the turn (the classic jibe) or before it (the switch-to-jibe). “Switch” means your feet are reversed: your usual front foot ends up at the back. A jibe is a change of direction that goes through downwind. A tack does the opposite: it goes through the wind, with your nose…

item.title: What is the best wind direction for wing foiling?
item.dc:creator: AFS
item.description: Best wind direction for wing foiling: how the wind shapes your speed and what to know about wind speed and how much wind you need. Tips from AFS.
item.content:encoded: In wingfoil, as in all water sports, the wind is our natural driving force. And depending on its direction, our speed varies according to our attitude to the wind. To get started and progress in wingfoiling, wind strength is extremely important. As a practitioner, you should favor moderate wind conditions, between 15 and 20 knots. Below this range, the wind is too light, making it difficult to take off and stay airborne. The ideal wind speed is 17-18 knots.
